questions.question: What is the 'Needle-in-a-Haystack' (NIAH) test designed to measure?
options: A model's ability to retrieve a specific fact from a very long context.
The speed of the model's tokenizer.
The number of tokens the model can generate per second.
If the model can find spelling errors in a long document.
questions.explanation: NIAH is the baseline test for long-context models, checking if a single fact buried deep in a 'haystack' of irrelevant text can still be retrieved correctly.

questions.question: What is the 'lost in the middle' effect in long-context models?
options: Models under-attend to content located in the middle of long inputs.
The model crashes when the answer is in the middle.
The model forgets the first sentence of the document.
The model's loss function fluctuates in the middle of training.
questions.explanation: Research has shown that LLMs are much better at remembering information at the very beginning or very end of their context window than information in the middle.

questions.question: Why is a 1M-token context window claim often misleading?
options: Usable capacity for reasoning and multi-hop tasks often degrades much earlier than retrieval capacity.
The model only uses 1,000 tokens in reality.
Tokens are counted differently by each vendor.
Context windows are only available during training.
questions.explanation: While a model might be able to find a single 'needle' at 1M tokens, its ability to reason over or summarize that entire 1M-token block is usually much lower.

questions.question: Which benchmark is considered the 2026 production standard for real-world long-context behavior?
questions.explanation: LongBench v2 provides a comprehensive set of tasks (QA, summarization, structural analysis) that simulate real-world usage of long-context models beyond simple retrieval.
